# Capability Jump × Deployment Rush: When Rapid Progress in Lean 4 AI Outpaces Validation of Formal Tools

**Problem:** Rapid progress in Lean 4 AI capability (from 12.5% to 60% in one generation) may cause premature deployment in safety-critical contexts before the validity of the capability signal (compilation rate as safety proxy) is established.

**Direction:** Model the compounding risk: (a) measure rate of capability improvement in Lean 4 benchmarks over time (using published results), (b) measure rate of validation research (papers studying safety signal validity), (c) compute the widening gap between capability claims and validation evidence. Survey researchers on deployment readiness criteria.

**Why it matters:** The pattern of AI capability outpacing safety validation is a general AI safety concern. This quantifies it specifically for formal verification AI, where premature deployment could lead to falsely verified safety-critical code.

**Relevant context:** VeriBench (ICML 2025) documents rapid capability progress. RAND calls for immediate benchmark development. But the papers studying whether Lean 4 compilation rate is a valid safety signal are sparse. This gap could lead to premature deployment.

title: Formal Verification × AI Agent Autonomy: Compounding Risk When Agents Self-Modify Verified Code

original_idea.body:
# Formal Verification × AI Agent Autonomy: Compounding Risk When Agents Self-Modify Verified Code

**Problem:** AI agents with code execution capabilities can modify code files. If an agent modifies formally verified code, the formal proof is invalidated. The combination of agentic autonomy (modifying code) and formal verification (proofs becoming stale) creates a compounding risk.

**Direction:** Design an experiment: create 10 formally verified Lean 4 programs. Deploy an AI agent (Claude Code or similar) to 'improve' each program under various task descriptions. Track whether: (a) agents modify code that has formal proofs, (b) agents update the corresponding proofs, (c) modifications invalidate proofs without updating them.

**Why it matters:** As AI agents become more autonomous in software development, their interaction with formally verified codebases creates risks that neither the AI safety community nor the formal methods community has studied. This is a genuine frontier compounding risk.

**Relevant context:** Claude Code executes code modification autonomously. Lean 4 proofs are invalidated by code changes. The interaction between agentic code modification and formal proof maintenance is unstudied.

title: Specification Arms Race: Formal Verification as a Target for Adversarial AI

original_idea.body:
# Specification Arms Race: Formal Verification as a Target for Adversarial AI

**Problem:** If formal verification is used to gate deployment of AI-generated code, adversarial AI systems could be trained to satisfy the formal verification checker while violating the intent. The combination of AI optimization and formal spec misalignment creates an adversarial dynamic not yet studied.

**Direction:** Train or prompt an LLM to generate code that: (a) formally verifies against a given spec, but (b) intentionally violates the informal intent of the spec (by exploiting spec under-specification). Measure how easy this is. Test whether code review can catch the violation after formal verification passes.

**Why it matters:** If formal verification can be satisfied adversarially, it fails as a security gateway. This is the formal methods analog of goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.

**Relevant context:** Adversarial examples against verification tools is a novel research direction. The general Goodhart's Law concern for AI safety measures is well-known. Applying it specifically to formal verification gating is not studied.

title: Formal Verification Confidence × Overreliance: Does Verification Success Reduce Human Code Review Quality?

original_idea.body:
# Formal Verification Confidence × Overreliance: Does Verification Success Reduce Human Code Review Quality?

**Problem:** When code is labeled as 'formally verified', human reviewers may reduce scrutiny due to overreliance on the verification certificate. This automation bias combined with formal verification false negatives creates a compounding risk.

**Direction:** Conduct a user study with 20 CS students. Present code review tasks: (a) code with no verification label, (b) code with 'formally verified' label but containing a subtle spec error. Measure time spent reviewing, error detection rate, and confidence ratings per condition. Test for automation bias effect.

**Why it matters:** Automation bias is documented for checklist-based safety systems (aviation). If 'formally verified' labels cause reviewers to trust AI-generated code with subtly wrong specs, the combination of false assurance + reduced scrutiny is worse than no formal verification.

**Relevant context:** Automation bias research (Parasuraman & Manzey 2010) is well-established. Its application to formal verification certification is novel. As formally verified AI code enters production, this compounding risk becomes practically important.

title: Can LLMs Generate Lean 4 Proofs for Non-Trivial Concurrency Safety Properties?

original_idea.body:
# Can LLMs Generate Lean 4 Proofs for Non-Trivial Concurrency Safety Properties?

**Problem:** Concurrency bugs (data races, deadlocks, TOCTOU vulnerabilities) are among the hardest to detect with existing tools. Whether LLMs can generate Lean 4 formal proofs for concurrency safety properties is completely unstudied.

**Direction:** Take 15 simple concurrent programs (producer-consumer, reader-writer, mutual exclusion). Write Lean 4 models of each. Ask LLMs to prove safety properties (mutual exclusion, absence of deadlock, absence of data race). Measure success rate and characterize failure modes.

**Why it matters:** Concurrency bugs are responsible for a significant fraction of security vulnerabilities. If LLM formal verification cannot handle concurrency, its applicability to the most dangerous bug class is limited.

**Relevant context:** Lean 4 concurrency modeling is nascent. TLA+ and Coq have been used for concurrency proofs. No study has attempted LLM-generated concurrency proofs in Lean 4. This is a critical gap given the prevalence of concurrency vulnerabilities.

original_idea.body:
# Formal Verification of Prompt Injection Defenses: Can Lean 4 Spec Capture Injection-Free Behavior?

**Problem:** Prompt injection is a key attack vector for LLM-based applications. Whether formal specifications can capture and verify 'prompt injection free' behavior as a formal safety property is a novel and unstudied question.

**Direction:** Define a formal model of prompt injection: a string processing function is injection-free if user-controlled input cannot influence the structure of system-controlled output. Attempt to express this in Lean 4 as a formal property. Ask LLMs to generate functions and proofs satisfying this property. Measure success rate.

**Why it matters:** If prompt injection can be formally specified, it becomes a verifiable property rather than a heuristic defense. This would represent a major advance in AI security from a formal methods perspective.

**Relevant context:** Prompt injection is a top security concern for LLM applications (OWASP AI). Formal methods have not been applied to prompt injection defense. This is a novel direction bridging formal verification and LLM security.

title: Lean 4 Proof Density as a Code Quality Metric: Does Proof Coverage Predict Runtime Reliability?

original_idea.body:
# Lean 4 Proof Density as a Code Quality Metric: Does Proof Coverage Predict Runtime Reliability?

**Problem:** Define 'proof density' as the ratio of formally verified statements to total code statements. Whether higher proof density predicts lower runtime failure rates (bugs per 1000 lines) is an empirical question not yet studied.

**Direction:** Collect 20 open-source projects with varying levels of formal verification (from zero to comprehensive). Compute proof density for each. Correlate with publicly available bug/CVE data. Test whether higher proof density significantly predicts lower bug rates.

**Why it matters:** If proof density correlates with reliability, it provides an actionable metric for safety-conscious development teams. This would empirically validate the assumption underlying the entire formal verification as safety paradigm.

**Relevant context:** Bug density metrics are standard in software engineering. Formal verification research focuses on capability, not on empirical correlation with real-world bug rates. This cross-over study would provide the first empirical validation of formal verification as a safety metric.

title: Transferability of Lean 4 Proof Strategies Across Isomorphic Problems

original_idea.body:
# Transferability of Lean 4 Proof Strategies Across Isomorphic Problems

**Problem:** If a proof strategy works for function A, will it work for isomorphic function B (same structure, different domain)? Whether Lean 4 proof strategies generalize across isomorphic problem structures — a form of analogical reasoning — is not tested.

**Direction:** Create 15 isomorphic problem pairs in Lean 4 (e.g., sorted list and sorted tree, integer bounds and float bounds). Ask LLMs to: (a) solve the first problem, then (b) reuse the same proof strategy for the isomorphic problem. Measure whether proof strategy transfer succeeds. Compare to solving each independently.

**Why it matters:** Human Lean experts reuse proof strategies across isomorphic structures. If LLMs cannot perform this analogical transfer, they are limited to syntactic pattern matching rather than mathematical reasoning, suggesting formal verification assistance will not scale.

**Relevant context:** Transfer of proof strategies (proof reuse, proof adaptation) is a research area in theorem proving. LLM analogical reasoning is studied in NLP. Combining these in Lean 4 is novel and directly relevant to scaling formal verification.

# Lean 4 as a Curriculum: Does Structured Learning of Lean 4 Tactics Improve LLM-Assisted Formal Verification?

**Problem:** Presenting Lean 4 tactic examples in a structured curriculum order (simple to complex) vs. a random order in few-shot prompts may affect LLM proof generation quality. Whether curriculum structure in prompting helps is unknown.

**Direction:** Create two prompting conditions: (a) 5 few-shot examples in order of increasing complexity (easy to hard), (b) 5 examples in random order, (c) 5 examples in decreasing complexity. Run on 40 VeriBench tasks. Measure compilation rate per condition. Test the curriculum hypothesis.

**Why it matters:** If curriculum order in few-shot examples improves Lean 4 proof generation, it is a zero-cost improvement to current prompting strategies. This would identify a new dimension of prompt engineering specific to formal verification.

**Relevant context:** Curriculum learning improves training efficiency for neural networks. Whether analogous curriculum structure in few-shot prompting improves in-context learning for formal verification has not been tested.

# Proof Generalization: Do LLMs That Solve Easy Lean 4 Problems Learn Transferable Strategies for Hard Problems?

**Problem:** The Self-Optimizing Trace Agent may be overfitting to easy VeriBench problems (the easy set accounts for most of the 60%). Whether success on easy problems transfers to hard problems (same agent, harder tasks) is not analyzed.

**Direction:** Stratify VeriBench into difficulty quartiles. Run the Self-Optimizing Trace Agent with varying amounts of easy-problem warm-up (0, 10, 20 easy problem traces in context). Measure whether warm-up on easy problems improves hard problem compilation rate. Test transfer generalization.

**Why it matters:** If easy problem warm-up does not improve hard problem performance, the path to closing the remaining 40% gap requires qualitatively different approaches, not just more iterations of the current architecture.

**Relevant context:** Self-Optimizing Trace Agent achieves ~60% overall but VeriBench has difficulty tiers. The easy set (42 problems) vs. HumanEval (51) vs. security (11) breakdown matters for interpreting the 60% figure.

title: Beyond Compilation Rate: What Other Metrics Should We Track for AI Formal Verification Progress?

original_idea.body:
# Beyond Compilation Rate: What Other Metrics Should We Track for AI Formal Verification Progress?

**Problem:** Compilation rate (the primary VeriBench metric) does not capture: proof quality, spec completeness, human review time, runtime behavior. A multi-dimensional metric suite for AI formal verification progress does not exist.

**Direction:** Propose and operationalize 5 additional metrics beyond compilation rate: (1) spec completeness score, (2) proof minimality ratio, (3) vacuity rate, (4) human review time per proof, (5) mutation survival rate. Measure all 5 on 30 VeriBench tasks across 3 LLMs. Publish as a multi-dimensional evaluation framework.

**Why it matters:** Single-metric optimization leads to goodharting. Compilation rate alone does not capture the safety-relevant dimensions of formal verification quality. A multi-dimensional dashboard would enable more honest progress tracking.

**Relevant context:** RAND (2026) calls for better benchmarks. VeriBench measures compilation and proof completion. VeriEquivBench measures equivalence. No paper combines these dimensions into a unified dashboard.

title: Formal Verification of Differential Privacy in AI Training: An End-to-End Experiment

original_idea.body:
# Formal Verification of Differential Privacy in AI Training: An End-to-End Experiment

**Problem:** Differential privacy (DP) guarantees for AI models are typically not formally verified — they rely on theoretical proofs that may have implementation bugs. Whether formal verification of DP in a simple AI training pipeline is tractable with LLM assistance is unknown.

**Direction:** Take a minimal DP-SGD implementation (Python, ~100 lines). Use LLM assistance to: (a) translate to Lean 4, (b) write formal spec capturing (ε,δ)-DP, (c) attempt proof. Measure whether proof completes, what the proof covers, and how long it takes with AI assistance.

**Why it matters:** Formally verified DP in AI training would represent a major AI safety milestone: mathematical proof that training preserves privacy. If it is tractable with current tools, it should be a near-term goal. If not, the gap must be characterized.

**Relevant context:** SampCert (Amazon) has Lean 4 proofs for DP mechanisms. DP-SGD is used in production (Google, Apple). No study has attempted end-to-end formal verification of a DP-SGD implementation with LLM assistance.

original_idea.body:
# Formal Verification Overhead Study: How Much Does Adding Lean 4 Proofs Increase Code Generation Time?

**Problem:** The practical cost of adding formal verification to AI-generated code (in time, compute, tokens) has not been measured. Whether the overhead is acceptable for production workflows is unknown.

**Direction:** Measure end-to-end time and token usage for: (a) standard code generation (no verification), (b) code generation + Lean 4 compilation, (c) code generation + full formal proof. Run on 40 VeriBench tasks. Compute median overhead per condition. Survey developers on acceptable overhead thresholds.

**Why it matters:** If formal verification adds 10x overhead, it will not be adopted in standard workflows regardless of safety benefits. If it adds only 2x, adoption becomes viable. This practical measurement is missing from the literature.

**Relevant context:** ATLAS generates 2.7K verified programs but reports compute cost only at batch level. No paper measures per-task overhead of formal verification in a developer workflow context. RAND calls for practical deployment.
